lessons.title: What Management Is and Why It Matters
lessons.body:
Defining management

Management is the process of getting work done efficiently and effectively through and with other people. Efficiency means using the fewest resources to achieve a result, while effectiveness means achieving the right result in the first place. A clinic that sees many patients quickly but misdiagnoses them is efficient but not effective.

Henri Fayol, a French mining engineer writing in 1916, described management as a set of functions. Modern textbooks usually group these into four:

  • Planning – setting goals and deciding how to reach them.

  • Organising – arranging people, tasks and resources into a structure.

  • Leading – motivating, communicating with and guiding people.

  • Controlling – monitoring performance and correcting deviations.

These functions apply to hospitals, start-ups, government offices and voluntary groups alike, which is why management is called a universal process. In practice they overlap: a ward manager may plan a roster, reorganise shifts and coach a new nurse in the same hour.
lessons.description: Understand what managers do and why management is described as a universal process.

lessons.title: Managerial Roles and Skills
lessons.body:
Mintzberg's managerial roles

Henry Mintzberg observed real managers and found that their work is fragmented and fast-paced. He grouped their activities into ten roles in three families:

  • Interpersonal – figurehead, leader and liaison.

  • Informational – monitor, disseminator and spokesperson.

  • Decisional – entrepreneur, disturbance handler, resource allocator and negotiator.

Katz's three skills

Robert Katz argued that managers need three kinds of skill. Technical skills are job-specific know-how and matter most for first-line supervisors. Human skills – working well with people – are important at every level. Conceptual skills, the ability to see the organisation as a whole and think in abstract terms, become more important the higher a manager rises.

A senior administrator rarely needs to perform a procedure, but must understand how every department fits together.

Reflect on your own role: which skills do you use most, and which will you need next?
lessons.description: Learn the roles managers play and the skills needed at each level of an organisation.

quiz.title: Introduction to management quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of the management functions, Mintzberg's roles and Katz's managerial skills.

lessons.title: Planning and Goal Setting
lessons.body:
Levels of planning

Plans cascade through an organisation. Strategic plans cover the whole organisation over several years. Tactical plans translate strategy into departmental actions, and operational plans set out day-to-day procedures, schedules and budgets.

SMART goals

A widely used checklist says goals should be:

  1. Specific – clearly state what is to be achieved.

  2. Measurable – include a number or observable result.

  3. Achievable – realistic given the resources available.

  4. Relevant – aligned with the wider mission.

  5. Time-bound – have a deadline.

Compare “improve patient satisfaction” with “raise the outpatient satisfaction score from 78% to 85% by March”. The second version tells everyone what success looks like and when to check.

Good planning also includes contingency plans – prepared responses for likely disruptions such as staff shortages or supply delays – so that the organisation can adapt without losing direction.
lessons.description: Learn how plans are structured and how to write goals that can be tracked.

lessons.title: Organising Structures
lessons.body:
Building a structure

Organising means dividing work into jobs, grouping jobs into departments and deciding who reports to whom. Key design elements include division of labour, chain of command, span of control (how many people report to one manager) and the degree of centralisation.

Common structures

  • Functional – grouped by specialism such as finance, nursing or pharmacy. Efficient, but departments can become silos.

  • Divisional – grouped by product, service line or region. Responsive to customers, but may duplicate resources.

  • Matrix – staff report to both a functional and a project manager. Flexible, but dual reporting can create conflict.

  • Team-based – cross-functional teams own a process end to end.

No structure is best in every situation. The right choice depends on size, strategy, environment and technology. Many hospitals combine a functional core with divisional service lines such as cardiology or women's health.
lessons.description: Compare common organisational structures and the trade-offs each involves.

lessons.title: Leading People
lessons.body:
From managing to leading

Leading is the function through which managers influence people to work towards goals. Early research looked for traits of great leaders; later work focused on behaviour and situation.

Leadership approaches

  • Transactional leadership exchanges rewards for performance and clarifies roles.

  • Transformational leadership inspires people with a shared vision and attends to individual development.

  • Situational leadership (Hersey and Blanchard) adjusts the mix of direction and support to the follower's readiness.

Motivation

Maslow proposed a hierarchy of needs from physiological to self-actualisation. Herzberg separated hygiene factors such as pay and working conditions, which prevent dissatisfaction, from motivators such as recognition and achievement, which build satisfaction. Vroom's expectancy theory adds that people are motivated when they believe effort leads to performance and performance leads to rewards they value.

Effective leaders combine these ideas: they remove frustrations, recognise good work and link daily tasks to a meaningful purpose.
lessons.description: Explore leadership styles and motivation theories that help managers guide teams.

quiz.title: Planning, organising and leading quiz
quiz.summary: Apply SMART goal setting, compare organisational structures and identify leadership and motivation theories in short scenarios.

lessons.title: What Is Operations Research?
lessons.body:
Origins and purpose

Operations research (OR) is the application of quantitative methods to help managers make better decisions. It grew out of military planning in Britain during the Second World War, when teams of scientists studied radar deployment and convoy sizes. After the war the same techniques spread to industry, logistics and healthcare.

The OR modelling process

  1. Define the problem – objectives, decisions and constraints.

  2. Build a model – usually a mathematical representation of the system.

  3. Collect data to estimate the model's parameters.

  4. Solve the model using an algorithm or simulation.

  5. Validate the results against reality.

  6. Implement the recommendation and monitor it.

A model is always a simplification. Its value lies in capturing the features that drive the decision while leaving out detail that does not change the answer. Managers should therefore understand a model's assumptions as well as its output.
lessons.description: Understand the origins of operations research and the modelling process it follows.

lessons.title: Formulating a Linear Programme
lessons.body:
The three parts of an LP

Linear programming (LP) finds the best way to allocate limited resources. Every LP has three parts:

  • Decision variables – the quantities you control, such as units of each product.

  • Objective function – a linear expression to maximise (profit) or minimise (cost).

  • Constraints – linear limits on resources, plus non-negativity of the variables.

A worked example

A workshop makes tables (x) and chairs (y). Each table earns 50 in profit and each chair 30. A table needs 4 hours of carpentry and a chair 3 hours, with 240 hours available. A table needs 2 hours of finishing and a chair 1 hour, with 100 hours available.

Maximise 50x + 30y subject to 4x + 3y ≤ 240, 2x + y ≤ 100, x ≥ 0 and y ≥ 0.

With two variables the model can be solved graphically: plot the constraints, shade the feasible region and evaluate the objective at each corner point. The optimum of an LP always occurs at a corner. Here the corners (0,0), (50,0), (30,40) and (0,80) give profits of 0, 2500, 2700 and 2400, so the best plan is 30 tables and 40 chairs.
lessons.description: Learn to express a resource-allocation problem as a linear programming model.

quiz.title: Introduction to operations research quiz
quiz.summary: Test your grasp of the OR modelling process and your ability to formulate and solve a simple linear programme.

lessons.title: Inventory Models and the EOQ
lessons.body:
Why inventory needs a model

Holding stock protects against shortages but ties up cash, space and risks expiry. Ordering frequently keeps stock low but increases ordering costs. The economic order quantity (EOQ) model finds the order size that minimises the total of these two costs.

The EOQ formula

If D is annual demand, S is the cost of placing one order and H is the cost of holding one unit for a year, then EOQ = √(2DS / H). At this quantity annual ordering cost equals annual holding cost.

For example, with D = 1,200 units, S = 50 and H = 3, EOQ = √(120,000 / 3) = 200 units, so about six orders a year.

Assumptions to remember

  • Demand is known and constant.

  • Lead time is known, and each order arrives all at once.

  • No quantity discounts or stock-outs.

Real systems add safety stock and a reorder point to cope with variable demand, but EOQ remains a useful starting benchmark.
lessons.description: Learn how the economic order quantity balances ordering and holding costs.

lessons.title: Queuing Theory Basics
lessons.body:
Modelling waiting lines

Queues form whenever demand for a service temporarily exceeds capacity – at pharmacy counters, call centres or emergency departments. Queuing theory describes these systems using the arrival rate (λ, customers per hour) and the service rate (μ, customers one server can handle per hour).

The single-server M/M/1 queue

With random (Poisson) arrivals, exponential service times and one server, the key results are:

  • Utilisation ρ = λ / μ, which must be below 1 for the queue to be stable.

  • Average number in the system L = ρ / (1 − ρ).

  • Average time in the system W = 1 / (μ − λ).

If 8 patients arrive per hour and a nurse can register 10 per hour, ρ = 0.8 and W = 0.5 hours. Raising arrivals to 9 per hour pushes W to a full hour.

As utilisation approaches 100%, waiting times rise sharply, not gradually.

This is why managers deliberately keep some spare capacity in services where delays are costly.
lessons.description: Understand how arrival and service rates determine waiting times.

lessons.title: Project Scheduling with CPM and PERT
lessons.body:
Projects as networks

A project can be drawn as a network of activities linked by their dependencies. The critical path method (CPM) identifies the longest path through the network, which sets the minimum project duration.

Steps in CPM

  1. List activities, durations and immediate predecessors.

  2. Do a forward pass to find each activity's earliest start and finish.

  3. Do a backward pass to find latest start and finish.

  4. Calculate slack (latest start minus earliest start). Activities with zero slack form the critical path.

Delaying a critical activity delays the whole project; activities with slack can slip a little without harm.

PERT for uncertain times

PERT uses three estimates for each activity – optimistic (a), most likely (m) and pessimistic (b) – and computes the expected time as (a + 4m + b) / 6. This lets managers estimate the probability of finishing by a given date, which is especially useful when commissioning a new ward or information system.
lessons.description: Learn to find a project's critical path and estimate uncertain activity times.

quiz.title: Inventory, queues and networks quiz
quiz.summary: Solve short problems on EOQ, single-server queues and critical path analysis.

lessons.title: What Is Ayurveda?
lessons.body:
The science of life

Ayurveda is a traditional system of medicine from the Indian subcontinent. Its name combines ayus (life) and veda (knowledge), so it is often translated as “the knowledge of life”.

Classical Ayurveda states two aims: to preserve the health of the healthy and to relieve disorders in those who are unwell. It therefore places strong emphasis on daily routine, diet and lifestyle.

Classical texts

Three texts, known together as the Brihat Trayi (the great three), form the foundation of the tradition:

  • Charaka Samhita – focused on internal medicine.

  • Sushruta Samhita – known for its detailed descriptions of surgery.

  • Ashtanga Hridaya by Vagbhata – a concise synthesis of earlier works.

The five elements

Ayurveda teaches that everything, including the body, is composed of five great elements (panchamahabhuta): space (akasha), air (vayu), fire (agni), water (jala) and earth (prithvi). Combinations of these elements give rise to the doshas, which are the focus of the next lesson.

This course describes these concepts as the tradition teaches them, as a foundation for further study.
lessons.description: Get an overview of Ayurveda's aims, classical texts and core worldview.

lessons.title: The Three Doshas
lessons.body:
Tridosha theory

Ayurveda describes three functional principles, the doshas, which govern the activities of body and mind. Each is formed from two of the five elements and is recognised by its qualities (gunas).

Vata

Formed from air and space. Its qualities are dry, light, cold, rough, subtle and mobile. Vata is described as governing movement: breathing, circulation, the passage of nerve impulses and elimination.

Pitta

Formed from fire with some water. Its qualities are hot, sharp, light, liquid and slightly oily. Pitta is described as governing transformation: digestion, metabolism, body heat and understanding.

Kapha

Formed from water and earth. Its qualities are heavy, cold, soft, oily, stable and slow. Kapha is described as governing structure, lubrication, stability and strength.

According to classical teaching, like increases like and opposites balance: dry, cold qualities are said to increase Vata, while warm, moist qualities are said to pacify it.

In balance, the doshas are said to sustain health; when disturbed, the tradition regards them as the basis of disorder.
lessons.description: Learn the qualities and functions of Vata, Pitta and Kapha as Ayurveda describes them.

quiz.title: Ayurveda foundations quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of Ayurveda's aims, the classical texts, the five elements and the qualities of the three doshas.

lessons.title: The Seven Dhatus and the Malas
lessons.body:
The seven dhatus

Ayurveda describes seven bodily tissues, or dhatus, which support and nourish the body. According to the classical sequence, each tissue is said to be nourished from the one before it:

  1. Rasa – plasma or the nutritive fluid.

  2. Rakta – blood.

  3. Mamsa – muscle.

  4. Meda – fat.

  5. Asthi – bone.

  6. Majja – marrow and nervous tissue.

  7. Shukra – reproductive tissue.

The malas

The tradition names three main waste products, or malas: purisha (faeces), mutra (urine) and sweda (sweat). Their regular and proper elimination is regarded as an important sign of balance.

Together, the doshas, dhatus and malas are called the three roots of the body. Classical texts describe health as a state in which all three are in balance, digestion is sound, and the senses, mind and self are content.
lessons.description: Understand the seven tissues and three waste products described in Ayurveda.

lessons.title: Agni and Ama
lessons.body:
Agni: the digestive fire

Agni is the Ayurvedic concept of the transforming fire responsible for digestion and metabolism. Classical texts describe many forms of agni; the chief one, jatharagni, is located in the digestive tract, while dhatvagnis are said to act within each tissue.

Four states of agni

  • Sama agni – balanced digestion, regarded as the ideal.

  • Vishama agni – irregular digestion, associated with Vata.

  • Tikshna agni – sharp, intense digestion, associated with Pitta.

  • Manda agni – slow, sluggish digestion, associated with Kapha.

Ama

When agni is weak, Ayurveda teaches that food is incompletely digested, producing ama, described as a heavy, sticky, undigested residue. Ama is regarded in the tradition as an underlying factor in many imbalances.

For this reason, Ayurvedic lifestyle guidance places great weight on eating when hungry, choosing suitable quantities, and avoiding eating again before the previous meal is digested.
lessons.description: Learn how Ayurveda views digestive fire and the concept of ama.

lessons.title: Prakriti and Vikriti
lessons.body:
Your constitution

Prakriti is the individual constitution. Ayurveda teaches that it is set at conception by the relative proportions of the three doshas and remains largely stable throughout life. It is said to shape a person's build, appetite, sleep, temperament and tendencies.

Types of prakriti

Classical texts describe seven types: three with one dominant dosha (Vata, Pitta or Kapha), three with two dominant doshas, and a rare balanced type in which all three are equal.

  • A Vata-predominant person is traditionally described as slender, quick and creative, with variable appetite.

  • A Pitta-predominant person is described as of medium build, focused and warm, with a strong appetite.

  • A Kapha-predominant person is described as sturdy, calm and steady, with a slower metabolism.

Vikriti

Vikriti refers to the current state of the doshas, which may differ from prakriti because of diet, season, age or stress. Ayurvedic practitioners assess both, since the tradition aims to guide a person back towards their own natural balance rather than towards a single ideal.
lessons.description: Understand how Ayurveda describes individual constitution and current state.

quiz.title: Dhatus, agni and prakriti quiz
quiz.summary: Test your knowledge of the seven dhatus, the malas, the states of agni and the concepts of prakriti and vikriti.

lessons.title: Origins and History of Siddha Medicine
lessons.body:
A Tamil medical tradition

Siddha medicine is a traditional system of medicine that developed in the Tamil-speaking region of southern India, particularly present-day Tamil Nadu. It is one of the recognised Indian systems of medicine and is today taught and practised in colleges and hospitals, especially in Tamil Nadu.

The Siddhars

The system is traditionally attributed to the Siddhars, a lineage of accomplished sages. Tradition speaks of eighteen principal Siddhars, with Agathiyar (Agastya) regarded as the foremost and often honoured as the founder of Siddha medicine. Others include Thirumoolar, Bogar, Theraiyar and Yugi.

Transmission of knowledge

Siddha knowledge was recorded in Tamil verse on palm-leaf manuscripts, often in a coded, poetic style that required a teacher's explanation. Many manuscripts have been collected, preserved and published in modern times.

  • The system covers medicine, yoga, alchemy and philosophy.

  • It gives particular importance to herbal, mineral and metal-based preparations.

  • Its texts combine health guidance with spiritual and ethical teaching.

This course presents Siddha concepts as the tradition describes them.
lessons.description: Learn where Siddha medicine comes from and how its knowledge was transmitted.

lessons.title: Philosophy: The Five Elements and 96 Thathuvams
lessons.body:
As in the universe, so in the body

A central idea of Siddha philosophy is expressed in the saying “Andathil ullathe pindam, pindathil ullathe andam” – what is in the universe is in the body, and what is in the body is in the universe. The human body is regarded as a microcosm of the cosmos.

Aimpootham: the five elements

Siddha teaches that all matter is composed of five elements (aimpootham):

  • Mann – earth.

  • Neer – water.

  • Thee – fire.

  • Vali – air.

  • Aagayam – space or ether.

The 96 thathuvams

The tradition describes the human being as made up of 96 thathuvams, or fundamental principles. They include the five elements, the sense organs, the organs of action, the humours, the tissues, states of consciousness and other physical and mental components. Studying these principles is intended to give the practitioner a complete picture of the person, integrating body, mind and spirit.
lessons.description: Understand the elemental theory and the principle that the body mirrors the universe.

quiz.title: Siddha origins and philosophy quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of the history of Siddha medicine, the Siddhars, the five elements and the concept of the 96 thathuvams.

Introduction to Siddha Medicine: Princip.section: The Three Humours and Seven Tissues

lessons.title: Mukkuttram: Vatham, Pitham and Kabam
lessons.body:
The three uyir thathukkal

Siddha medicine describes three vital humours, called uyir thathukkal (life-sustaining principles). When they are disturbed, they are called mukkuttram, the three faults.

  • Vatham – associated with air and space; described as governing movement, breathing and nervous function.

  • Pitham – associated with fire; described as governing digestion, heat, vision and transformation.

  • Kabam – associated with water and earth; described as governing stability, lubrication and strength.

Proportion in health

Siddha texts describe the humours in health in the proportion of 1 : ½ : ¼ for Vatham, Pitham and Kabam. This proportion is also used as a reference point in pulse reading, which is taught in the advanced course on Siddha diagnosis.

Each humour has subtypes

The tradition describes ten types of Vatham, five of Pitham and five of Kabam, each with a specific location and function. For example, pranan is the type of Vatham associated with breathing.

Health, in the Siddha view, is the state in which the three humours are in their proper proportion.
lessons.description: Learn how Siddha medicine describes the three humours and their balance.

lessons.title: Udal Thathukkal: The Seven Physical Constituents
lessons.body:
Seven physical constituents

Siddha medicine describes seven bodily constituents, the udal thathukkal, which are said to support and sustain the body:

  1. Saaram – the nutritive essence, described as giving vitality and nourishment.

  2. Senneer – blood, described as giving colour, strength and nourishment to the tissues.

  3. Oon – muscle, described as giving shape and allowing movement.

  4. Kozhuppu – fat, described as lubricating the joints and tissues.

  5. Enbu – bone, described as supporting the body and posture.

  6. Moolai – marrow, described as filling the bones and giving strength.

  7. Sukkilam / Suronitham – the male and female reproductive constituents.

Relationship with the humours

According to Siddha teaching, the humours act upon the tissues. An increase or decrease in a humour is said to affect particular tissues, and the tradition describes characteristic features of each tissue in excess or in deficiency.

Diet, daily routine (naal ozhukkam) and seasonal routine (kaala ozhukkam) are emphasised in Siddha teaching as ways to maintain the balance of humours and tissues.
lessons.description: Learn the seven body tissues described in Siddha medicine and their functions.

quiz.title: Humours and tissues quiz
quiz.summary: Test your knowledge of Vatham, Pitham and Kabam, their healthy proportion, and the seven udal thathukkal.

lessons.title: Levels of Organisation and Anatomical Language
lessons.body:
From atoms to organism

Anatomy studies the structure of the body; physiology studies how those structures function. The body is organised in levels of increasing complexity: chemical, cellular, tissue, organ, organ system and organism.

There are four basic tissue types: epithelial (covering and lining), connective (support and binding), muscle (movement) and nervous (communication).

The anatomical position

All directional terms refer to the anatomical position: standing upright, facing forward, arms at the sides with palms facing forward.

  • Superior / inferior – towards the head / towards the feet.

  • Anterior / posterior – towards the front / towards the back.

  • Medial / lateral – towards the midline / away from the midline.

  • Proximal / distal – closer to / farther from the point of attachment of a limb.

The body can be divided by the sagittal plane into left and right, the frontal (coronal) plane into front and back, and the transverse plane into upper and lower parts.
lessons.description: Learn how the body is organised and the standard terms used to describe it.

lessons.title: Homeostasis and Feedback
lessons.body:
A stable internal environment

Homeostasis is the maintenance of relatively stable internal conditions – such as body temperature, blood glucose and blood pressure – despite changes outside the body. The term was coined by the physiologist Walter Cannon.

Components of a control system

  1. A receptor detects a change in a variable.

  2. A control centre, often in the brain, compares it with a set point.

  3. An effector produces a response that changes the variable.

Negative and positive feedback

Most homeostatic mechanisms use negative feedback, where the response reverses the original change. When body temperature rises, the hypothalamus triggers sweating and dilation of skin blood vessels, and temperature falls back towards normal. After a meal, rising blood glucose stimulates insulin release, which helps cells take up glucose.

Positive feedback amplifies a change until an endpoint is reached. Examples include uterine contractions during childbirth, reinforced by oxytocin, and the formation of a platelet plug during blood clotting.
lessons.description: Understand how the body keeps its internal environment stable.

quiz.title: Body organisation and homeostasis quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of levels of organisation, directional terms, body planes and feedback mechanisms.

lessons.title: The Heart and Circulation
lessons.body:
Structure of the heart

The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: two atria that receive blood and two ventricles that pump it out. Valves keep blood moving in one direction – the tricuspid and mitral (bicuspid) valves between atria and ventricles, and the pulmonary and aortic valves at the ventricular exits.

Two circulations

Deoxygenated blood returns from the body through the venae cavae to the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle and is pumped through the pulmonary arteries to the lungs. This is the pulmonary circulation.

Oxygenated blood returns through the pulmonary veins to the left atrium, flows to the left ventricle and is pumped into the aorta for distribution to the body – the systemic circulation. The left ventricle has a thicker wall because it pumps against higher pressure.

The conduction system

Each heartbeat starts at the sinoatrial (SA) node, the natural pacemaker. The impulse spreads across the atria to the atrioventricular (AV) node, then through the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres to the ventricles. Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by stroke volume.
lessons.description: Trace the path of blood through the heart and the two circulations.

lessons.title: Breathing and Gas Exchange
lessons.body:
The airway

Air passes through the nose or mouth, pharynx, larynx and trachea, which divides into two main bronchi. These branch repeatedly into bronchioles, ending in millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli, surrounded by capillaries.

Mechanics of breathing

During inspiration the diaphragm contracts and flattens, and the external intercostal muscles lift the ribs. The chest cavity enlarges, pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. Quiet expiration is largely passive: the muscles relax and the elastic lungs recoil.

Gas exchange

In the alveoli, oxygen diffuses from air into blood and carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into air, each moving down its partial pressure gradient. Most oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin in red blood cells, while most carbon dioxide travels as bicarbonate ions.

Breathing is controlled by respiratory centres in the brainstem, which respond mainly to the level of carbon dioxide in the blood rather than to oxygen.
lessons.description: Learn how air moves into the lungs and how oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged.

quiz.title: Cardiovascular and respiratory systems quiz
quiz.summary: Test your knowledge of blood flow through the heart, the conduction system, breathing mechanics and gas exchange.

lessons.title: The Hospital as an Organisation
lessons.body:
Types of hospital

Hospitals can be classified by ownership (public, private for-profit, not-for-profit or charitable), by level of care (primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary) and by scope (general or specialty). Teaching hospitals add education and research to patient care.

Governance and structure

A governing board or trust sets strategic direction and holds executives accountable. Beneath it, an executive team – typically a chief executive, medical director, nursing director and finance director – runs day-to-day operations.

Hospital departments are commonly grouped into three families:

  • Clinical services – medicine, surgery, paediatrics, obstetrics and emergency care.

  • Clinical support services – laboratory, radiology, pharmacy and blood bank.

  • Administrative and hotel services – finance, human resources, medical records, housekeeping, dietary and facilities management.

Hospitals are often described as professional bureaucracies: highly trained clinicians have considerable autonomy, so administrators must lead through collaboration and shared goals as much as through formal authority.
lessons.description: Understand how hospitals are classified, governed and structured.

lessons.title: Core Functions of Hospital Administration
lessons.body:
What administrators manage

Hospital administrators ensure that clinicians have the people, space, equipment, information and money they need to deliver safe care.

  • Human resources – workforce planning, credentialing, rostering, training and staff welfare.

  • Materials management – procurement, inventory and distribution of drugs and consumables, often using ABC and VED analysis to prioritise items.

  • Patient flow – admissions, bed management, discharge planning and reducing avoidable delays.

  • Health information – medical records, coding, data privacy and electronic health record systems.

  • Facilities and biomedical engineering – maintenance, utilities and equipment safety.

  • Finance – budgeting, billing and cost control.

Key performance indicators

Administrators monitor indicators such as bed occupancy rate, average length of stay, bed turnover rate, outpatient waiting time and staff turnover. No single indicator tells the whole story: very high occupancy, for example, can signal efficiency but also a lack of surge capacity.
lessons.description: Explore the key operational responsibilities of hospital administrators.

quiz.title: Hospital administration fundamentals quiz
quiz.summary: Test your knowledge of hospital classification, governance, departmental structure and operational indicators.

lessons.title: Defining and Measuring Quality
lessons.body:
Dimensions of quality

The US Institute of Medicine's 2001 report Crossing the Quality Chasm described six aims: care should be safe, effective, patient-centred, timely, efficient and equitable. These aims remain a useful checklist for any quality programme.

Donabedian's model

Avedis Donabedian proposed that quality can be assessed through three linked categories:

  • Structure – the setting and resources, such as staffing ratios, equipment and qualifications.

  • Process – what is actually done, such as the proportion of patients given timely antibiotics.

  • Outcome – the effects on health, such as infection rates, readmissions, mortality and patient experience.

Good structure makes good process more likely, and good process makes good outcomes more likely. Process measures are often preferred for improvement work because they are easier to influence and quicker to change, while outcome measures need careful risk adjustment before hospitals are compared.
lessons.description: Learn the frameworks used to define and measure healthcare quality.

lessons.title: Quality Improvement Tools
lessons.body:
The PDCA cycle

The Plan–Do–Check–Act cycle, popularised by W. Edwards Deming, structures improvement as a series of small tests of change:

  1. Plan – define the problem, set an aim and predict what the change will achieve.

  2. Do – test the change on a small scale and collect data.

  3. Check (or Study) – compare results with the prediction.

  4. Act – adopt, adapt or abandon the change, then begin the next cycle.

Supporting tools

  • Fishbone (Ishikawa) diagrams organise possible causes of a problem.

  • Pareto charts show that a few causes often account for most problems.

  • Run and control charts distinguish random variation from real change over time.

  • Process maps reveal delays, duplication and hand-off points.

Approaches such as Lean, which targets waste, and Six Sigma, which targets variation, build on the same principles.
lessons.description: Apply PDCA and common quality tools to improve hospital processes.

lessons.title: Patient Safety and Accreditation
lessons.body:
A systems view of error

James Reason's Swiss cheese model shows that harm usually occurs when weaknesses in several layers of defence line up, rather than because of one careless individual. Safety therefore depends on designing robust systems and fostering a just culture, in which staff feel able to report errors and near misses without fear of unfair blame.

Common safety practices

  • Correct patient identification using at least two identifiers.

  • Surgical safety checklists before, during and after operations.

  • Hand hygiene and infection-prevention bundles.

  • Structured handover tools such as SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation).

  • Root cause analysis of serious incidents.

Accreditation

Accreditation bodies such as Joint Commission International and India's National Accreditation Board for Hospitals and Healthcare Providers (NABH) assess hospitals against published standards. Preparing for accreditation encourages documented processes, regular audits and continuous improvement.
lessons.description: Understand how systems thinking, incident reporting and accreditation support safe care.

quiz.title: Quality and patient safety quiz
quiz.summary: Apply Donabedian's model, PDCA, quality tools and patient-safety principles to hospital scenarios.

lessons.title: What Pharmacology Studies
lessons.body:
Defining the field

Pharmacology is the study of how drugs interact with living systems. Clinical pharmacology applies this knowledge to the safe and effective use of medicines in people.

The subject has two broad branches:

  • Pharmacokinetics – what the body does to the drug: absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion.

  • Pharmacodynamics – what the drug does to the body: its mechanism of action and effects.

Drug names

Every drug has a chemical name describing its structure, a generic (non-proprietary) name such as paracetamol, and one or more brand names chosen by manufacturers. Generic names are preferred in prescribing and teaching because they are consistent worldwide and help avoid confusion.

Classification

Drugs may be grouped by therapeutic use (for example antihypertensives), by mechanism (beta-blockers) or by chemical structure. Many drugs belong to more than one group, so understanding the mechanism is more useful than memorising a single label.
lessons.description: Learn the scope of pharmacology and the main ways drugs are named and classified.

lessons.title: Pharmacokinetics: ADME
lessons.body:
The journey of a drug

Absorption

Absorption is the movement of a drug from its site of administration into the bloodstream. Drugs given orally may undergo first-pass metabolism in the gut wall and liver before reaching the systemic circulation. Bioavailability is the fraction of a dose that reaches the circulation unchanged; for intravenous drugs it is 100%.

Distribution

Once in the blood, drugs distribute to tissues. Many bind to plasma proteins such as albumin, and only the unbound fraction is pharmacologically active. Barriers such as the blood–brain barrier restrict entry to some tissues.

Metabolism

The liver is the main site of metabolism. Phase I reactions, often carried out by cytochrome P450 enzymes, modify the drug; phase II reactions conjugate it to make it more water-soluble.

Excretion

Most drugs and metabolites are excreted by the kidneys, with some eliminated in bile. The half-life is the time for plasma concentration to fall by half; it takes roughly four to five half-lives to reach steady state or to eliminate most of a drug.
lessons.description: Understand how drugs are absorbed, distributed, metabolised and excreted.

quiz.title: Pharmacology foundations quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of drug nomenclature, classification and the four stages of pharmacokinetics.

lessons.title: How Drugs Act: Receptors and Response
lessons.body:
Drug targets

Most drugs act by binding to specific target proteins: receptors, enzymes, ion channels or transporters. The strength of binding is called affinity, and the ability to activate the receptor once bound is called efficacy.

Agonists and antagonists

  • An agonist binds to a receptor and activates it, mimicking a natural signal.

  • A partial agonist activates the receptor but produces less than the maximum response.

  • An antagonist binds without activating the receptor and blocks the action of agonists. Competitive antagonism can be overcome by raising the agonist concentration.

Dose–response and safety margin

Potency refers to the amount of drug needed to produce an effect, whereas efficacy refers to the maximum effect achievable. The therapeutic index compares the dose that causes toxicity with the dose that produces the desired effect. Drugs with a narrow therapeutic index, such as warfarin, digoxin and lithium, require careful monitoring because the gap between benefit and harm is small.
lessons.description: Learn the receptor concepts that explain how drugs produce their effects.

lessons.title: Adverse Drug Reactions and Interactions
lessons.body:
Adverse drug reactions

An adverse drug reaction (ADR) is a harmful, unintended response to a medicine used normally. A classic classification separates:

  • Type A (augmented) – predictable from the drug's pharmacology, dose-related and common, such as bleeding with anticoagulants.

  • Type B (bizarre) – unpredictable and not dose-related, such as allergic reactions and anaphylaxis.

Health professionals are encouraged to report suspected ADRs to national pharmacovigilance programmes, which detect safety signals that clinical trials may miss.

Drug interactions

Pharmacokinetic interactions occur when one drug changes the absorption, distribution, metabolism or excretion of another – for example, enzyme inhibitors can raise levels of drugs metabolised by the same cytochrome P450 enzyme. Pharmacodynamic interactions occur when drugs have additive or opposing effects, such as combining two sedating medicines.

Interactions can also involve foods and herbal products; grapefruit juice, for instance, inhibits an enzyme that metabolises several drugs. Always take a full medication history, including non-prescription products.
lessons.description: Recognise the main types of adverse drug reactions and drug interactions.

lessons.title: Safe Medication Practice
lessons.body:
Why medication errors happen

Medication errors can occur at any stage: prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, administering or monitoring. Common contributors include look-alike and sound-alike drug names, illegible or ambiguous orders, interruptions and incomplete patient information.

The rights of medication administration

A widely taught checklist reminds practitioners to confirm the:

  1. right patient,

  2. right drug,

  3. right dose,

  4. right route,

  5. right time, and

  6. right documentation.

Many curricula add the right reason, right response and the patient's right to refuse.

System safeguards

  • Check allergies and use two patient identifiers before every administration.

  • Use independent double checks for high-alert medicines such as insulin and anticoagulants.

  • Avoid error-prone abbreviations in orders.

  • Use barcode scanning and electronic prescribing where available.

When in doubt, stop and clarify with the prescriber or pharmacist before giving a medicine.
lessons.description: Apply the rights of medication administration and other practices that prevent errors.

quiz.title: Pharmacodynamics and medication safety quiz
quiz.summary: Apply receptor concepts, ADR classification, interaction mechanisms and safe administration practices to clinical scenarios.

lessons.title: Yoga and Yoga Therapy
lessons.body:
The roots of yoga

Yoga is a practice tradition from ancient India. The word comes from the Sanskrit root yuj, meaning to join or yoke. The Yoga Sutras attributed to Patanjali define yoga as the stilling of the fluctuations of the mind and describe an eight-limbed path (ashtanga):

  1. Yama – ethical restraints.

  2. Niyama – personal observances.

  3. Asana – steady, comfortable posture.

  4. Pranayama – regulation of the breath.

  5. Pratyahara – withdrawal of the senses.

  6. Dharana – concentration.

  7. Dhyana – meditation.

  8. Samadhi – absorption.

What is yoga therapy?

Yoga therapy adapts these practices to an individual's needs and health situation. It is a complementary approach that supports general well-being alongside, not instead of, medical care. Research suggests yoga may help some people with stress, flexibility and certain types of chronic low back pain, but responses vary.
lessons.description: Understand the roots of yoga and what yoga therapy aims to do.

lessons.title: Practising Safely
lessons.body:
Safety first

Yoga is generally considered safe when practised sensibly, but injuries can occur, especially when people force postures or practise beyond their current ability.

General guidelines

  • Practise on an empty or light stomach, ideally two to three hours after a main meal.

  • Use a non-slip mat and wear comfortable clothing.

  • Move slowly and never force a stretch; mild sensation is acceptable, sharp pain is a signal to stop.

  • Breathe steadily through the nose and avoid holding the breath during postures.

  • Use props such as blocks, straps, cushions and chairs to adapt poses.

When to seek advice first

Consult a doctor before starting or changing practice if you are pregnant, have high blood pressure, glaucoma, heart disease, recent surgery, osteoporosis, or back or joint problems. Some postures, such as strong inversions and deep backbends, are unsuitable for certain conditions.

A good practice leaves you feeling calmer and more comfortable than when you began.

Learning from a qualified teacher helps ensure correct technique.
lessons.description: Learn the safety principles that make yoga practice appropriate for everyday life.

quiz.title: Yoga foundations and safety quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of Patanjali's eight limbs, the aims of yoga therapy and safe practice guidelines.

lessons.title: Gentle Asanas for Daily Practice
lessons.body:
A simple daily sequence

Asanas are traditionally described as postures that should be steady and comfortable. The following gentle poses are suitable for most beginners when done with care.

  1. Tadasana (mountain pose) – stand tall with feet grounded, arms by the sides; builds postural awareness.

  2. Marjaryasana–bitilasana (cat–cow) – on hands and knees, alternately round and gently arch the spine with the breath.

  3. Balasana (child's pose) – kneel and fold forward, resting the forehead on the floor or a cushion.

  4. Setu bandhasana (bridge pose) – lying on the back with knees bent, lift the hips gently.

  5. Supta matsyendrasana (supine twist) – lying down, let the knees fall to one side while the shoulders stay on the floor.

Tips

Hold each pose for a few comfortable breaths, repeat on both sides where relevant and rest between poses. Those with knee or wrist discomfort can use padding, and anyone with back problems should seek guidance on twists and backbends. Consistency matters more than intensity: ten minutes daily is more beneficial than an occasional long session.
lessons.description: Learn a short sequence of gentle postures suitable for most beginners.

lessons.title: Breathing Practices (Pranayama)
lessons.body:
Working with the breath

Pranayama refers to yogic breathing practices. Slow, gentle breathing is widely used as a relaxation technique.

Diaphragmatic breathing

Sit or lie comfortably with one hand on the chest and one on the abdomen. Breathe in through the nose so the abdomen rises more than the chest, then breathe out slowly. This is the foundation for other practices.

Nadi shodhana (alternate nostril breathing)

Using the right thumb and ring finger, close one nostril at a time: inhale through the left, exhale through the right, inhale through the right, exhale through the left. This completes one round. Keep the breath smooth and unforced.

Bhramari (humming bee breath)

Inhale through the nose and, while exhaling, make a steady, soft humming sound. Many people find the vibration and lengthened exhalation calming.

  • Stop if you feel dizzy or breathless.

  • Avoid breath retention and forceful techniques without a teacher, especially with heart or blood pressure conditions or during pregnancy.
lessons.description: Learn three calming breathing practices and how to do them safely.

lessons.title: Relaxation and Mindful Awareness
lessons.body:
Shavasana and deep relaxation

Shavasana, the corpse pose, is practised lying on the back with arms and legs relaxed and eyes closed. It is commonly used at the end of a session to allow the body to rest. A cushion under the knees can make it more comfortable for the lower back.

Body scan

In a body scan, attention moves slowly from the toes to the head, noticing sensations in each area without trying to change them. Where tension is noticed, the practitioner simply lets it soften with the out-breath.

Short daily meditation

  1. Sit comfortably with the spine upright.

  2. Close the eyes or rest the gaze downwards.

  3. Rest attention on the natural breath at the nostrils or abdomen.

  4. When the mind wanders, gently return to the breath without judgement.

  5. Begin with five minutes and extend gradually.

Relaxation practices can support stress management and sleep habits. People with significant anxiety, depression or trauma should practise with guidance from a qualified professional, as introspective practices can sometimes bring up difficult feelings.
lessons.description: Learn simple relaxation and meditation practices to include in daily life.

quiz.title: Everyday yoga practices quiz
quiz.summary: Identify the correct technique and safety precautions for the asanas, breathing practices and relaxation methods covered.

lessons.title: The Strategic Management Process
lessons.body:
What strategy means

Strategy is an organisation's long-term plan for creating value and competing successfully. Strategic management is the ongoing process of formulating, implementing and evaluating that plan.

The core stages

  1. Direction setting – a vision describes the desired future; a mission states the organisation's purpose and whom it serves; values guide behaviour.

  2. Environmental analysis – examining external opportunities and threats and internal strengths and weaknesses.

  3. Strategy formulation – choosing where to compete and how to win.

  4. Implementation – aligning structure, culture, resources and systems.

  5. Evaluation and control – measuring results and adjusting course.

Henry Mintzberg noted that realised strategy is often a mix of deliberate strategy, planned in advance, and emergent strategy, which arises from patterns of action as managers respond to events. Good strategists plan carefully but stay alert to what is actually working.
lessons.description: Understand the stages of strategic management and the role of vision and mission.

lessons.title: Analysing the Environment
lessons.body:
External analysis

PESTEL scans the macro-environment: Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental and Legal factors. For a hospital group this might include health policy reforms, ageing populations and digital health regulation.

Michael Porter's five forces model explains industry profitability through:

  • rivalry among existing competitors,

  • the threat of new entrants,

  • the threat of substitutes,

  • the bargaining power of buyers, and

  • the bargaining power of suppliers.

Internal analysis

The resource-based view holds that lasting advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and well organised (the VRIO test).

Bringing it together with SWOT

A SWOT matrix summarises internal Strengths and Weaknesses alongside external Opportunities and Threats. Its real value comes from the next step: matching strengths to opportunities and addressing weaknesses that expose the organisation to threats.
lessons.description: Apply PESTEL, Porter's five forces and SWOT to analyse an organisation's position.

quiz.title: Strategic analysis quiz
quiz.summary: Identify stages of the strategic management process and apply PESTEL, five forces and SWOT to short cases.

lessons.title: Competitive and Corporate Strategies
lessons.body:
Business-level strategy

Porter identified three generic strategies:

  • Cost leadership – being the lowest-cost provider in the industry.

  • Differentiation – offering something customers value enough to pay a premium for.

  • Focus – serving a narrow segment through either cost or differentiation.

Porter warned that firms trying to do everything risk being “stuck in the middle”, although some organisations do combine low cost with differentiation through innovation.

Corporate-level strategy

Corporate strategy decides which businesses to be in. The Ansoff matrix sets out four growth routes: market penetration, market development, product development and diversification, with risk rising as the organisation moves further from its existing products and markets.

Growth can be pursued organically, through alliances and joint ventures, or through mergers and acquisitions. Each route trades off speed, control, cost and risk, and the right choice depends on the capabilities the organisation already has.
lessons.description: Distinguish business-level strategies from corporate-level growth choices.

lessons.title: Rational and Behavioural Decision Making
lessons.body:
The rational model

The classical model assumes a decision maker who defines the problem, identifies all alternatives, evaluates each against clear criteria and chooses the one that maximises value.

Bounded rationality

Herbert Simon argued that real managers face limited time, information and cognitive capacity. They therefore satisfice – choosing the first option that is good enough – rather than optimising.

Common cognitive biases

  • Anchoring – relying too heavily on the first number seen.

  • Confirmation bias – seeking information that supports an existing view.

  • Overconfidence – overestimating the accuracy of one's judgements.

  • Escalation of commitment – continuing to invest in a failing course because of past investment.

  • Groupthink – a cohesive group suppressing dissent to maintain harmony.

Debiasing techniques include appointing a devil's advocate, considering the opposite, running a pre-mortem that imagines the decision has failed, and separating idea generation from evaluation.
lessons.description: Compare the rational decision model with how managers actually decide under uncertainty.

lessons.title: Decision Trees and Expected Value
lessons.body:
Structuring decisions under risk

A decision tree maps choices and uncertain events in sequence. Squares represent decisions, circles represent chance events with probabilities, and the end of each branch shows a payoff.

Expected monetary value

The expected monetary value (EMV) of a chance node is the sum of each outcome multiplied by its probability. The tree is solved by rolling back from right to left, choosing the branch with the best EMV at each decision node.

Suppose opening a new diagnostic centre yields a profit of 500 with probability 0.6 and a loss of 200 with probability 0.4. EMV = 0.6 × 500 + 0.4 × (−200) = 220. If the alternative, expanding an existing site, has a certain profit of 180, the new centre has the higher EMV.

Limits of EMV

  • EMV ignores the decision maker's attitude to risk.

  • Probabilities are often subjective estimates.

  • Sensitivity analysis shows how far estimates can change before the preferred option switches.
lessons.description: Use decision trees and expected monetary value to compare risky alternatives.

quiz.title: Strategic choice and decision making quiz
quiz.summary: Apply generic strategies, the Ansoff matrix, bias awareness and expected value calculations to managerial scenarios.

lessons.title: How Money Flows in Healthcare
lessons.body:
Who pays for care?

Healthcare is financed through a mix of sources: government budgets funded by taxes, social health insurance funded by payroll contributions, private insurance premiums, employer schemes and out-of-pocket payments made directly by patients. The balance between these sources varies widely from country to country.

How providers are paid

  • Fee-for-service – a payment for each service delivered; encourages volume.

  • Capitation – a fixed amount per enrolled person per period; encourages cost control but can discourage needed care.

  • Case-based or DRG payment – a set amount per admission based on diagnosis group.

  • Salary and global budgets – common in public systems.

  • Value-based payment – links part of the payment to quality and outcomes.

Each method creates different incentives. Managers need to understand them because the payer mix shapes a hospital's revenue, its cash flow and even its clinical pathways.
lessons.description: Understand the main payers and payment methods that fund healthcare services.

lessons.title: Costs, Budgets and Break-even
lessons.body:
Classifying costs

Fixed costs, such as rent and salaried staff, do not change with activity in the short term. Variable costs, such as consumables, rise with each patient served. Direct costs can be traced to a specific service; indirect costs or overheads, such as administration, are shared and must be allocated.

Budgets

An operating budget plans revenue and expenses for the year, while a capital budget plans major purchases such as imaging equipment. Comparing actual results with budget and investigating variances is a core control activity.

Break-even analysis

The break-even volume is the number of cases at which total revenue equals total cost:

Break-even volume = Fixed costs ÷ (Price per case − Variable cost per case)

If a dialysis unit has fixed costs of 300,000 a year, receives 2,500 per session and spends 1,000 per session on variable costs, it breaks even at 200 sessions. The difference between price and variable cost is called the contribution margin.
lessons.description: Learn cost classifications and how budgets and break-even analysis support decisions.

quiz.title: Healthcare finance basics quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of payment methods, cost behaviour, budgeting and break-even calculations.

Healthcare Finance & Insurance Essential.section: Health Insurance and the Revenue Cycle

lessons.title: Key Health Insurance Concepts
lessons.body:
How insurance pools risk

Insurance works by pooling: many people pay a premium into a common fund, which pays the costs of the few who need care. Pooling only works if both healthy and unhealthy people join. When mainly high-risk people buy cover, premiums rise and healthy members leave – a problem called adverse selection.

Cost-sharing terms

  • Deductible – the amount the insured person pays before cover begins.

  • Co-payment – a fixed amount paid per service.

  • Co-insurance – a percentage of the cost shared by the insured person.

  • Sum insured – the maximum the policy will pay in a period.

  • Exclusions and waiting periods – conditions not covered, or covered only after a set time.

Cost-sharing helps limit moral hazard, the tendency to use more services when someone else pays. Policies should nevertheless be read carefully, because terms differ between insurers and schemes.
lessons.description: Learn the vocabulary of health insurance and how cost-sharing works.

lessons.title: Claims and the Revenue Cycle
lessons.body:
The revenue cycle

The revenue cycle covers every administrative and clinical step that turns a service into payment. Weaknesses at any stage lead to delays, denials and lost income.

  1. Registration and eligibility checks – capture accurate demographics and verify insurance cover.

  2. Pre-authorisation – obtain approval from the insurer or third-party administrator (TPA) for planned procedures.

  3. Charge capture and coding – record services and assign diagnosis and procedure codes such as ICD-10.

  4. Claim submission – send a complete, accurate claim with supporting documents.

  5. Adjudication and payment – the payer reviews, approves, partly pays or denies the claim.

  6. Denial management and collections – correct and resubmit denied claims and collect patient balances.

Cashless versus reimbursement

In a cashless claim the insurer pays the network hospital directly after authorisation. In a reimbursement claim the patient pays first and then claims the money back. Tracking measures such as days in accounts receivable and the claim denial rate helps managers keep the cycle healthy.
lessons.description: Follow a patient account from registration to final payment.

quiz.title: Health insurance and revenue cycle quiz
quiz.summary: Apply insurance terminology and revenue-cycle steps to realistic billing scenarios.

lessons.title: How Medical Words Are Built
lessons.body:
Word parts

Most medical terms come from Greek and Latin and are built from a small set of parts. Once you learn the parts, you can work out the meaning of thousands of words.

  • Word root – the core meaning, often a body part: cardi (heart), gastr (stomach), hepat (liver).

  • Prefix – placed before the root to modify it: brady- (slow), tachy- (fast), hyper- (above), hypo- (below).

  • Suffix – placed at the end to indicate a condition or procedure: -itis (inflammation), -ectomy (surgical removal), -ology (study of).

  • Combining vowel – usually o, added to ease pronunciation.

Putting it together

Gastroenterology breaks into gastr/o (stomach) + enter/o (intestine) + -logy (study of). The combining vowel is generally dropped before a suffix that begins with a vowel, which is why we write gastritis, not “gastroitis”.

A useful habit is to define a term starting with the suffix, then the prefix, then the root: pericarditis means inflammation of the area around the heart.
lessons.description: Learn to break medical terms into roots, prefixes and suffixes.

lessons.title: Common Prefixes and Suffixes
lessons.body:
High-frequency prefixes

  • a-, an- – without or absence of (anaemia).

  • dys- – difficult or abnormal (dyspnoea, difficult breathing).

  • endo- – within (endoscopy).

  • peri- – around (perianal).

  • poly- – many or much (polyuria).

Suffixes for conditions and procedures

  • -algia – pain (neuralgia).

  • -emia or -aemia – blood condition (hyperglycaemia).

  • -megaly – enlargement (hepatomegaly).

  • -scopy – visual examination (colonoscopy).

  • -ostomy – creation of an opening (colostomy).

  • -otomy – cutting into (tracheotomy).

Pay close attention to similar-looking suffixes: -ectomy, -ostomy and -otomy describe very different procedures. Note also that British and American spellings differ, for example haemorrhage and hemorrhage; follow the convention used in your workplace.
lessons.description: Build a working vocabulary of high-frequency prefixes and suffixes.

quiz.title: Medical word building quiz
quiz.summary: Break down and define medical terms using roots, prefixes, suffixes and combining vowels.

Medical Terminology for Health Professio.section: Body Systems Vocabulary and Safe Abbreviations

lessons.title: Terms Across the Body Systems
lessons.body:
Roots by body system

Learning roots by body system helps you connect terminology with anatomy.

  • Cardiovascular – cardi/o (heart), angi/o and vas/o (vessel), arteri/o (artery), phleb/o (vein).

  • Respiratory – pneum/o (lung or air), bronch/o (bronchus), rhin/o (nose).

  • Digestive – or/o (mouth), col/o (colon), chol/e (bile).

  • Urinary – nephr/o and ren/o (kidney), cyst/o (bladder).

  • Nervous – neur/o (nerve), encephal/o (brain), myel/o (spinal cord or bone marrow).

  • Musculoskeletal – oste/o (bone), arthr/o (joint), my/o (muscle).

Greek and Latin pairs

Many organs have two roots. Greek roots are often used for diseases and procedures, while Latin roots appear in anatomical adjectives: nephritis (kidney inflammation) but renal artery.

Try decoding osteoarthritis, cholecystectomy and cystoscopy using the roots above. Then check your answers against a medical dictionary, and keep a personal glossary of new terms as you meet them.
lessons.description: Recognise key word roots for the major body systems.

lessons.title: Abbreviations and Documentation Safety
lessons.body:
Why abbreviations matter

Abbreviations save time, but misread abbreviations are a recognised cause of medication errors. Many organisations, including The Joint Commission in the United States, publish “do not use” lists.

Abbreviations to avoid

  • U for unit – can be mistaken for 0 or 4. Write “unit”.

  • IU – can be misread as IV or 10. Write “international unit”.

  • QD and QOD – easily confused with each other. Write “daily” and “every other day”.

  • Trailing zero (5.0) – may be read as 50. Write 5.

  • Missing leading zero (.5) – may be read as 5. Write 0.5.

  • MS, MSO4 and MgSO4 – can mean morphine or magnesium sulphate. Write the full drug name.

Good documentation habits

Use only abbreviations approved by your organisation, write legibly, spell out drug names and clarify any order you cannot read with certainty. Clear terminology protects patients as much as clinical skill does.
lessons.description: Use abbreviations accurately and avoid those known to cause errors.

quiz.title: Body systems and abbreviations quiz
quiz.summary: Identify body-system word roots and recognise safe and unsafe abbreviations in clinical documentation.

lessons.title: What Is Dravyaguna?
lessons.body:
The study of substances

Dravyaguna is the branch of Ayurveda that studies medicinal substances. Its name joins dravya (substance) and guna (quality or property). It describes plants, minerals and animal products according to their properties and the actions attributed to them in classical texts.

Classical works group plants in several ways. The Charaka Samhita arranges them into fifty groups (mahakashaya) of ten plants each, according to their traditional actions. Later texts called nighantus, such as the Bhavaprakasha Nighantu, act as lexicons listing names, synonyms and properties.

Identification and quality

Because many plants share local names, correct identification is essential. Modern Dravyaguna study includes:

  • botanical names and plant families,

  • the part used, such as root, bark, leaf, fruit or seed,

  • collection season and storage, and

  • recognising adulterants and substitutes.

Medicinal plants can interact with conventional medicines and may be unsuitable in pregnancy or other situations, so their use should always be guided by a qualified practitioner.
lessons.description: Understand the scope of Dravyaguna and its place within Ayurveda.

lessons.title: Rasa, Guna, Virya, Vipaka and Prabhava
lessons.body:
The five pharmacological principles

Rasa – taste

Ayurveda recognises six tastes: madhura (sweet), amla (sour), lavana (salty), katu (pungent), tikta (bitter) and kashaya (astringent). Each is said to be formed from two elements and to affect the doshas: sweet, sour and salty are said to pacify Vata, while bitter, pungent and astringent are said to pacify Kapha.

Guna – qualities

Physical qualities such as heavy or light, oily or dry, and hot or cold. Classical texts list twenty such qualities in ten pairs.

Virya – potency

Usually described as either ushna (heating) or sheeta (cooling).

Vipaka – post-digestive effect

The taste a substance is said to take on after digestion: sweet, sour or pungent.

Prabhava – special action

A specific effect that cannot be explained by the other four properties. Classical texts use it to explain why two substances with similar properties are said to act differently.

Together these five properties form the framework used to describe any substance in Dravyaguna.
lessons.description: Learn the five properties through which Ayurveda describes every substance.

quiz.title: Dravyaguna principles quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of the scope of Dravyaguna and the concepts of rasa, guna, virya, vipaka and prabhava.

lessons.title: Amalaki and Haridra
lessons.body:
Amalaki (Phyllanthus emblica)

Amalaki, also called Indian gooseberry or amla, belongs to the family Phyllanthaceae. The fruit is the part used.

  • Rasa – five tastes, all except salty, with sour predominant.

  • Virya – cooling (sheeta).

  • Vipaka – sweet (madhura).

Classical texts regard it as a rasayana, or rejuvenative, and it is one of the three fruits in the well-known formulation Triphala, alongside haritaki and bibhitaki. Modern analysis shows the fruit is a rich source of vitamin C.

Haridra (Curcuma longa)

Haridra, or turmeric, belongs to the ginger family, Zingiberaceae. The rhizome is used.

  • Rasa – bitter and pungent.

  • Virya – heating (ushna).

  • Vipaka – pungent (katu).

Ayurveda traditionally describes haridra in the context of skin health and the balancing of Kapha. Its main pigment, curcumin, is the subject of ongoing scientific research, but research findings should not be read as proof of treatment effects.
lessons.description: Study the traditional properties of amalaki and turmeric as described in Ayurveda.

lessons.title: Guduchi, Ashwagandha and Tulsi
lessons.body:
Guduchi (Tinospora cordifolia)

A climbing shrub whose stem is used. Its rasa is bitter and astringent, its virya heating and its vipaka sweet. Classical texts call it amrita and describe it as a rasayana that balances all three doshas.

Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera)

A member of the nightshade family, Solanaceae, whose root is mainly used. Its rasa is described as bitter, astringent and sweet, its virya heating and its vipaka sweet. The tradition regards it as a rasayana and associates it with strength and with balancing Vata and Kapha.

Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum)

Holy basil, a member of the mint family, Lamiaceae, is valued in Indian households and grown near many homes and temples. The leaves are used. Its rasa is pungent and bitter and its virya heating, and it is traditionally associated with the respiratory system and with balancing Kapha and Vata.

Safety note

  • Herbs are biologically active and can cause side effects.

  • Some may interact with prescribed medicines.

  • Quality varies between products; adulteration and contamination occur.

  • Use should be guided by a qualified practitioner, especially in pregnancy, childhood and chronic illness.

lessons.title: Food and Daily Routine in Ayurveda
lessons.body:
Ahara: food as a pillar of life

Ayurveda names three supporting pillars of life (trayopastambha): ahara (food), nidra (sleep) and brahmacharya (regulated conduct). Of these, food receives the most attention in classical texts.

Classical guidelines for eating

  • Eat warm, freshly prepared food.

  • Eat when the previous meal has been digested and genuine hunger is present.

  • Eat an appropriate quantity; one traditional guide is to fill the stomach one-half with solid food, one-quarter with liquid and leave one-quarter empty.

  • Eat in a calm setting, neither too fast nor too slowly, with attention on the meal.

  • Include all six tastes over the course of the day.

Dinacharya: the daily routine

Dinacharya is the recommended daily routine. It traditionally includes waking early, around brahma muhurta before sunrise, cleaning the teeth and scraping the tongue, gargling, self-massage with oil (abhyanga), exercise suited to one's strength, bathing, and meals at regular times.

The tradition holds that a regular rhythm of eating, sleeping and activity supports balance of the doshas.
lessons.description: Learn the Ayurvedic principles of wholesome eating and daily routine.

lessons.title: Why Seasons Matter
lessons.body:
Six seasons

Ritucharya means “seasonal regimen”. Classical texts divide the year into six seasons (ritus) of about two months each, based on the climate of the Indian subcontinent:

  1. Shishira – late winter.

  2. Vasanta – spring.

  3. Grishma – summer.

  4. Varsha – monsoon.

  5. Sharad – autumn.

  6. Hemanta – early winter.

Two halves of the year

The first three seasons form adana kala, the period when the sun moves northward (uttarayana). The tradition teaches that the sun's heat draws strength from living beings, so physical strength is said to decline across this period.

The last three form visarga kala, the period of the southward sun (dakshinayana), when the moon's cooling influence is said to restore strength. Strength is described as lowest in early summer and monsoon, and highest in winter.

Seasons in other climates differ, so learners are encouraged to apply the principles to their local weather.
lessons.description: Understand how Ayurveda divides the year and relates seasons to strength.

quiz.title: Ayurvedic diet and routine quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of the three pillars of life, classical eating guidelines, dinacharya and the six seasons.

lessons.title: Winter and Spring Regimens
lessons.body:
Hemanta and Shishira: the cold seasons

In winter, Ayurveda teaches that digestive fire is strong because the body conserves heat. Classical texts therefore recommend nourishing, warm and unctuous foods, including grains, dairy, sesame and appropriate amounts of sweet, sour and salty tastes.

  • Regular oil massage and exercise.

  • Warm water for bathing and drinking.

  • Warm clothing and protection from cold wind.

  • Avoiding light, dry and cold foods that are said to aggravate Vata.

Vasanta: spring

According to the tradition, Kapha accumulated during winter becomes liquefied by the warming sun in spring, which may weaken digestion. The recommendations shift accordingly:

  • Favour light, easily digested foods and older grains such as barley.

  • Prefer bitter, pungent and astringent tastes.

  • Reduce heavy, oily, sour and sweet foods.

  • Exercise regularly and avoid sleeping during the day.

Classical texts also describe cleansing therapies for this season, which are carried out only under a qualified practitioner's supervision.
lessons.description: Learn the diet and lifestyle guidance Ayurveda gives for the cold seasons and spring.

lessons.title: Summer and Monsoon Regimens
lessons.body:
Grishma: summer

In summer, strength is said to be low and the sun's heat drying. The tradition advises choosing foods that are sweet, cool, light and liquid:

  • Drink adequate cool (not ice-cold) water and fluids such as buttermilk.

  • Favour rice, milk, ghee and juicy fruits.

  • Limit pungent, sour, salty and very hot foods, and reduce strenuous exercise.

  • A short daytime rest is considered acceptable in this season.

Varsha: monsoon

During the rains, Ayurveda teaches that digestion is at its weakest and that Vata is aggravated by the damp, cool conditions. Recommended practices include:

  • Eating light, warm, freshly cooked food.

  • Using boiled and cooled water.

  • Including old grains and small amounts of sour and salty tastes to support digestion.

  • Avoiding overexertion and keeping the body dry and warm.

These recommendations mirror common-sense food hygiene in wet weather, when contaminated water is a well-known risk.
lessons.description: Learn the seasonal guidance for the hot and rainy months.

lessons.title: Autumn and Seasonal Transitions
lessons.body:
Sharad: autumn

Ayurveda teaches that Pitta accumulated during the monsoon is aggravated when the autumn sun becomes strong after the rains. The recommended regimen therefore favours cooling, calming choices:

  • Sweet, bitter and astringent tastes.

  • Light foods such as rice, green gram and ghee in suitable amounts.

  • Avoiding excess heat, sun exposure, curd, oily and very pungent foods.

  • Enjoying cool evenings and moonlight, which classical texts specifically mention.

Ritu sandhi: the junction between seasons

The tradition describes a transitional period of about fourteen days – the last week of one season and the first week of the next – called ritu sandhi. During this time, classical texts advise gradually letting go of the old season's habits and slowly adopting the new ones, rather than changing abruptly.

Gradual change is a recurring theme in Ayurveda: the body is said to adapt best to steady, moderate shifts.
lessons.description: Understand autumn guidance and the concept of ritu sandhi between seasons.

quiz.title: Seasonal regimens quiz
quiz.summary: Match diet and lifestyle recommendations to each of the six seasons and explain the concept of ritu sandhi.

lessons.title: The Diagnostic Approach in Siddha
lessons.body:
Diagnosis in the Siddha tradition

Siddha diagnosis aims to identify which humour – Vatham, Pitham or Kabam – is disturbed, how it has affected the tissues and what factors have contributed. The practitioner considers the person as a whole, including constitution, age, season, diet, habits and surroundings.

Envagai Thervu

The central method is Envagai Thervu, the eight-fold examination. Its eight components are:

  1. Naadi – pulse.

  2. Sparisam – touch.

  3. Naa – tongue.

  4. Niram – colour or complexion.

  5. Mozhi – voice and speech.

  6. Vizhi – eyes.

  7. Malam – stool.

  8. Moothiram – urine.

Each component is interpreted according to the three humours. Findings are considered together rather than in isolation.

In modern Siddha practice these methods are taught alongside basic clinical examination. Anyone with symptoms of a serious condition should be evaluated by a qualified medical professional.
lessons.description: Understand the principles behind Siddha diagnosis and where the eight-fold examination fits.

lessons.title: Naadi: Pulse Examination
lessons.body:
The central place of naadi

Among the eight methods, naadi (pulse) is traditionally given the greatest importance, and its interpretation is said to require long training under an experienced teacher.

Method as traditionally taught

  • The pulse is felt at the radial artery on the wrist, commonly on the right hand in men and the left hand in women.

  • The practitioner places the index, middle and ring fingers side by side over the artery, just below the wrist.

  • The index finger is said to perceive Vatham, the middle finger Pitham and the ring finger Kabam.

  • Examination is preferably done in the early morning, with the person rested and before food.

Interpretation

Siddha texts describe the healthy pulse as having Vatham, Pitham and Kabam in the proportion 1 : ½ : ¼. Changes in this pattern, and qualities of the pulse such as its speed, strength and character, are interpreted as indications of which humour is dominant or disturbed.

The texts compare characteristic pulse movements to the gait of animals and birds, such as a swan, peacock or frog, as a way of describing them.

Traditional pulse reading describes humoral balance; it is not a substitute for measuring pulse rate, rhythm and blood pressure in clinical practice.
lessons.description: Learn how the Siddha tradition describes reading the pulse.

quiz.title: Envagai Thervu foundations quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of the aims of Siddha diagnosis, the eight components of Envagai Thervu and traditional pulse examination.
