lessons.title: Sparisam, Naa, Niram, Mozhi and Vizhi
lessons.body:
Five observational examinations

These components rely on careful observation and touch. As traditionally described, their findings are grouped according to the three humours.

Sparisam – touch

The practitioner notes the temperature, moisture and texture of the skin. Classical descriptions associate coolness with Vatham, warmth with Pitham and a cool, moist feel with Kabam.

Naa – tongue

The colour, coating, moisture, cracks and taste sensation are examined. A dry, cracked tongue is traditionally linked with Vatham, a red or yellowish tongue with Pitham, and a pale, coated, moist tongue with Kabam.

Niram – colour

Complexion of the skin, nails and other areas is observed. Darkish tones are associated with Vatham, yellowish or reddish tones with Pitham and pale tones with Kabam.

Mozhi – voice

Pitch, strength and clarity of speech are assessed. A moderate voice is associated with Vatham, a high-pitched or sharp voice with Pitham and a low, heavy voice with Kabam.

Vizhi – eyes

The colour of the conjunctiva, moisture, discharge and sensitivity to light are observed and interpreted in the same humoral framework.
lessons.description: Learn how touch, tongue, complexion, voice and eyes are interpreted in Siddha diagnosis.

lessons.title: Malam and Moothiram: Stool and Urine
lessons.body:
Malam – stool

The practitioner asks about or observes the colour, consistency, quantity and frequency of stool. Traditional descriptions associate dry, hard stool with Vatham, yellowish, loose stool with Pitham and pale, sticky stool with Kabam.

Moothiram – urine

Urine examination has two parts in the Siddha tradition:

  • Neerkkuri – observation of the urine's colour, odour, froth, quantity and deposits.

  • Neikkuri – the oil-drop test, a method distinctive to Siddha.

The neikkuri method

As traditionally described, the person is advised to eat a balanced meal the previous evening. The first urine of the morning is collected in a clean vessel, and after a short interval a drop of sesame oil is placed gently on its surface in good light. The way the drop spreads is then observed:

  • spreading in a snake-like pattern is associated with Vatham,

  • spreading like a ring is associated with Pitham, and

  • remaining like a pearl is associated with Kabam.

Rapid spreading or sinking of the drop is described in classical texts as indicating greater difficulty in management. Neikkuri is a traditional assessment method and is interpreted alongside the other seven components.
lessons.description: Understand how stool and urine examination, including neikkuri, are described in Siddha.

quiz.title: Eight-fold examination practice quiz
quiz.summary: Interpret traditional Envagai Thervu findings for each component and match them to the humour they are associated with.

lessons.title: What Is Varmam?
lessons.body:
Vital points of the body

Varmam (also written varma) is a branch of the Siddha tradition concerned with vital points on the body. Siddha texts describe these points as sites where vital energy, called pranan or vaasi, is concentrated.

The tradition holds that the same knowledge has two applications: as a martial art, where striking a point was said to cause injury, and as a therapy (varma maruthuvam), where skilled manipulation of the points is used to restore the flow of vital energy.

Origins

Varmam is traditionally attributed to the Siddhar Agathiyar. It has been preserved particularly in the southern districts of Tamil Nadu, such as Kanyakumari, and in neighbouring Kerala, where it is linked with martial practices such as Adimurai and Kalaripayattu.

Transmission

For centuries the knowledge was passed down within families and from teacher (aasaan) to student, often in secret, with Tamil verse texts that required the teacher's explanation. Today it is also taught as part of formal Siddha education.
lessons.description: Understand the meaning, origins and scope of the Varmam tradition.

lessons.title: Classification of Varmam Points
lessons.body:
How many points?

Different Varmam texts give different counts, but a commonly cited classification lists 108 varmam points, divided into:

  • 12 Padu varmam – described as the most vital points, where injury was regarded as especially serious.

  • 96 Thodu varmam – described as points affected by touch or lesser force.

Other texts describe additional categories, such as thattu varmam, nokku varmam and thadavu varmam, according to the kind of contact involved.

Locating points

Points are located by their relationship to anatomical landmarks and are measured using viral alavu, a system of finger-breadth units taken from the person's own fingers. Using the individual's own proportions allows the measurement to adapt to different body sizes.

Distribution

The tradition groups points by region: head and neck, chest and abdomen, back, upper limbs and lower limbs. Each point has a name, a location, a described relationship with the humours and a traditional therapeutic use.
lessons.description: Learn how the tradition counts, classifies and locates varmam points.

quiz.title: Varmam foundations quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of the origins of Varmam, its dual traditions and the classification of varmam points.

lessons.title: Therapeutic Techniques
lessons.body:
Varma maruthuvam

In the therapeutic tradition, a trained practitioner applies specific kinds of pressure to varmam points in order, as the tradition describes it, to restore the flow of vital energy and relieve discomfort. Techniques are chosen according to the point, the person and the purpose.

Common techniques

  • Pressure – steady pressure applied with a finger or thumb, in a defined direction and for a defined duration.

  • Thadaval – gentle stroking or massage along a region, sometimes with medicated oils.

  • Adangal – techniques traditionally described for counteracting the effects of a varmam injury.

  • Supportive measures – such as external oils, bandaging or fomentation, as used in Siddha practice.

The tradition describes the intensity of pressure in terms of fractions of a unit called maathirai, and stresses that the amount of pressure and its direction matter as much as the location.

Varmam therapy is today most commonly sought for musculoskeletal complaints such as joint stiffness and sprains, alongside other Siddha measures.
lessons.description: Learn the main manual techniques used in traditional Varmam therapy.

lessons.title: Safety, Training and Ethics
lessons.body:
Why training matters

The Varmam tradition itself emphasises that its points can harm as well as help. Incorrect force at the wrong site is described in the texts as dangerous, which is why the knowledge was guarded and taught only to trusted students after long training.

Principles of safe practice

  • Learn only under a qualified, experienced teacher; this introductory course does not prepare you to treat anyone.

  • Take a full history and consider when a person needs medical assessment first, for example after trauma, with suspected fractures, loss of consciousness or chest pain.

  • Avoid applying pressure over broken skin, recent injuries, suspected fractures or areas of acute swelling.

  • Use particular caution in pregnancy, in older adults with fragile bones and in people taking blood-thinning medicines.

  • Obtain informed consent and explain what the therapy involves.

A complementary role

Varmam is a traditional therapy and should complement, not replace, medical assessment and care. Practitioners should make no claims of cure and should refer promptly when symptoms are serious, worsening or unexplained.
lessons.description: Understand why Varmam must be learned from qualified teachers and practised responsibly.

quiz.title: Varmam therapy principles quiz
quiz.summary: Test your understanding of traditional Varmam techniques and the safety and ethical principles of practice.

lessons.title: The Role of Clinical Nutrition
lessons.body:
Nutrition as part of care

Clinical nutrition is the assessment and management of nutrition in people with, or at risk of, disease. It forms part of care for many chronic conditions, including diabetes, cardiovascular disease and chronic kidney disease, alongside medical treatment.

Malnutrition includes both undernutrition and overnutrition. Undernutrition is common in hospitals and is associated with slower wound healing, higher infection risk and longer stays. Overweight and obesity increase the risk of type 2 diabetes, hypertension and some cancers.

Macronutrients and micronutrients

  • Carbohydrates provide about 4 kcal per gram and are the body's main energy source.

  • Proteins provide about 4 kcal per gram and supply amino acids for tissue repair.

  • Fats provide about 9 kcal per gram and supply essential fatty acids.

  • Vitamins and minerals are needed in small amounts for metabolism, immunity and bone health.

Diet plans for chronic conditions should be individualised by a qualified dietitian or clinician, taking into account medical history, medicines, culture and preferences.
lessons.description: Understand what clinical nutrition covers and how malnutrition affects patients.

lessons.title: Nutrition Assessment
lessons.body:
The ABCD approach

  • Anthropometry – height, weight, body mass index (BMI = weight in kg ÷ height in m²), waist circumference and recent weight change.

  • Biochemistry – laboratory values such as blood glucose, HbA1c, lipid profile, kidney function and haemoglobin.

  • Clinical assessment – physical signs such as muscle wasting, oedema and skin or hair changes, together with medical history.

  • Dietary assessment – 24-hour recall, food frequency questionnaires or food diaries.

Screening tools

Screening quickly identifies people who need a full assessment. Validated tools include the Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), the Nutritional Risk Screening 2002 (NRS-2002) and the Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA) for older adults.

BMI has limits: it does not distinguish muscle from fat, and some populations, including many South Asian groups, face higher metabolic risk at lower BMI values. For this reason waist circumference and clinical judgement should be considered alongside it.
lessons.description: Learn the ABCD framework and common screening tools for assessing nutritional status.

quiz.title: Clinical nutrition foundations quiz
quiz.summary: Check your understanding of macronutrients, malnutrition and the ABCD nutrition assessment framework.

lessons.title: Nutrition in Type 2 Diabetes
lessons.body:
Goals of dietary management

In type 2 diabetes, nutrition therapy aims to support blood glucose control, achieve or maintain a healthy weight and reduce cardiovascular risk. There is no single “diabetic diet”; several eating patterns can be effective when tailored to the individual.

Common principles

  • Choose high-fibre carbohydrates such as whole grains, legumes, vegetables and whole fruits over refined starches and sugary drinks.

  • Distribute carbohydrate across the day and keep portions consistent, especially for people on glucose-lowering medicines.

  • Include lean protein and healthy fats from nuts, seeds and vegetable oils.

  • Limit saturated fat, processed foods and added sugars.

Useful tools

The plate method fills half the plate with non-starchy vegetables, a quarter with protein and a quarter with carbohydrate foods. Glycaemic index describes how quickly a food raises blood glucose, and carbohydrate counting helps match intake to treatment.

Diet changes should be coordinated with the care team, because changes in eating can affect how medicines work and may require monitoring.
lessons.description: Understand the dietary principles commonly recommended for people with type 2 diabetes.

lessons.title: Diets for Hypertension and Heart Health
lessons.body:
The DASH eating pattern

The Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet was tested in clinical trials in the 1990s and shown to lower blood pressure. It emphasises:

  • vegetables, fruits and whole grains,

  • low-fat dairy products,

  • fish, poultry, legumes, nuts and seeds, and

  • limited red meat, sweets and sugar-sweetened drinks.

The pattern is rich in potassium, magnesium, calcium and fibre. Combining DASH with reduced sodium intake lowers blood pressure further than either change alone. The World Health Organization recommends that adults consume less than 5 g of salt a day.

Heart-healthy fats

Replacing saturated and trans fats with unsaturated fats from vegetable oils, nuts and fish is associated with improved blood lipid levels. Practical steps include cooking at home more often, reading food labels for sodium and fat, and reducing processed and fried foods. People with kidney disease or on certain medicines may need to limit potassium, so advice must be individualised.
lessons.description: Learn the key features of the DASH eating pattern and heart-healthy diets.

lessons.title: Nutrition in Chronic Kidney Disease
lessons.body:
Why diet matters in CKD

Healthy kidneys regulate fluid, electrolytes and waste products. As kidney function declines in chronic kidney disease (CKD), these substances can build up, so dietary advice changes with the stage of disease and the type of treatment.

Nutrients commonly reviewed

  • Protein – moderate restriction may be advised in earlier stages not on dialysis, while people on dialysis generally need more protein because some is lost during treatment.

  • Sodium – limiting salt helps control blood pressure and fluid retention.

  • Potassium – may need to be limited if blood levels are high, since high potassium affects heart rhythm.

  • Phosphorus – often restricted in later stages to protect bone and blood vessel health.

  • Fluid – may be limited for people on dialysis.

Restrictions are based on blood test results and should never be applied without guidance, because unnecessary restriction can lead to malnutrition. A renal dietitian works with the patient to balance these limits against adequate energy intake and food enjoyment.
lessons.description: Understand why diets in chronic kidney disease are individualised by stage.

quiz.title: Diet planning for chronic conditions quiz
quiz.summary: Apply dietary principles for type 2 diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease to patient case scenarios.
